7e368ba833.q: What is the biggest mistake financial advisors make when a high-net-worth client walks through the door?
7e368ba833.a: If you're asking what to do differently when someone with 10, 20, or 50 million dollars walks through the door, you've already messed it up. The issue lies in prescribing solutions before understanding the symptoms. Many advisors grew up in product distribution and pitch products immediately, but ultra-high-net-worth clients have been pitched every product under the sun and want to be understood and served in a way that actually helps them reach their goals.

a24a59801a.q: Why should financial advisors avoid leading with products when working with high-net-worth individuals?
a24a59801a.a: Leading with product creates small ticket, transactional sales and captures only a fraction of investable assets. A Triad member from a firm that sold 10 to 30 million of annuity business annually had zero clients with over one million in investable assets despite working with hundreds of families. After switching to a financial planning process-driven approach instead of product-driven, that same firm brought on clients with 10 million, 6 million, and 3 million in investable assets, and will bring on approximately 140 to 150 million in total assets this year.

6f68440225.q: Why should financial advisors stick to a 60 to 90 minute first meeting even with high-net-worth prospects?
6f68440225.a: Most humans are mentally tapped after 60 to 90 minutes; spending more time starts to overwhelm people and they check out. If you extend a first meeting to three hours because a prospect has 5 to 10 million, it psychologically signals that you don't specialize in this level of wealth and have low demand. Your time should be perceived as valuable, and breaking your time commitment rules based on account size actually costs you clients rather than gaining them.

101dea3f8a.q: What qualification should a high-net-worth prospect meet before an advisor moves to a second meeting?
101dea3f8a.a: An advisor should ask the prospect at the end of the first meeting: if you feel confident (at least a seven out of 10) that you'd be open and willing to work with us if we fix these problems, would you commit to that? If they cannot say yes to that without dancing around it or citing obstacles like a son-in-law managing assets, there is no point in moving forward. Proceeding anyway leads to the hamster wheel salesperson effect with 4 to 10+ appointments chasing the prospect.
